summary:
Grenada criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Section 430 of the Criminal Code addresses "grossly indecent acts" between men and Section 431 addresses "unnatural crime"; both provisions remain in force. The United States Department of State reported in its 2023 human rights report that these laws are not enforced in practice.

No legal gender recognition is available, so a trans visitor's documents will reflect the sex marker assigned at birth or by another jurisdiction, with no domestic route to amend them.

No statutory anti-discrimination protections cover sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBTIQ people in Grenada face discrimination in housing, education, employment and access to public services.

Fear of prosecution under Sections 430 and 431 inhibits LGBTIQ people from reporting crimes to the police, which weakens the practical value of police protection even where officers do not pursue prosecutions.

The 2023 United States Department of State report records no arbitrary killings, torture or forced disappearances in Grenada.

GrenCHAP has provided services to marginalised groups for more than fifteen years, working with LGBT+ people, people living with HIV, sex workers and vulnerable youth; it is the principal documented point of support for a visitor seeking community-based assistance.

An October 2024 stakeholder report by The Advocates for Human Rights, Khaleem Ali and GrenCHAP, submitted for the Universal Periodic Review, documents the legal and social situation of LGBTIQ+ people in Grenada, including the Sections 430 and 431 provisions.

Grenada is a small island society in which social visibility is high; the sources describe sustained social discrimination alongside formal non-enforcement of the criminal provisions.
tangentialFactors:
Grenada's LGBTIQ legal framework is under active international scrutiny. The October 2024 stakeholder submission to the Universal Periodic Review assembles the criminal provisions, the absence of legal gender recognition and the pattern of discrimination for consideration by UN member states.

The United States Department of State's 2023 human rights reporting on Grenada pairs the criminalisation finding with a record of no arbitrary killings, torture or disappearances, indicating an official hostility profile that is legislative and social rather than custodial.

The gap between the statute book and enforcement is the defining feature of the country's position: conduct criminalised on paper is not prosecuted, but the existence of the offence shapes how LGBTIQ people interact with police and public institutions.

Community infrastructure is comparatively durable for a small jurisdiction, with GrenCHAP sustaining services to LGBT+ people, people living with HIV, sex workers and vulnerable youth across more than fifteen years.
localsOnly:
Residents who are LGBTIQ face discrimination in housing, education, employment and public services, with no anti-discrimination statute available as a remedy.

Fear of prosecution under Sections 430 and 431 deters LGBTIQ residents from reporting crime to the police, a barrier that persists despite the reported non-enforcement of those sections.

Legal gender recognition does not exist, so residents cannot change identity documents to reflect their gender identity.

GrenCHAP has served marginalised groups for more than fifteen years, including LGBT+ people, people living with HIV, sex workers and vulnerable youth, and is a documented source of community support and of human rights documentation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The current sources state the text of Sections 430 and 431 but do not set out the penalties those sections carry, so the sentence exposure attached to a conviction is not sourced here.

No source in this inventory addresses marriage or partner recognition for same-sex couples in Grenada; that question is unresolved rather than answered in the negative.

No source records whether any prosecution under Sections 430 or 431 has ever been brought, so the statement that the provisions are unenforced rests on the United States Department of State's 2023 assessment rather than on a prosecution-by-prosecution record.

Nothing in the inventory addresses border screening, entry refusal on the basis of gender identity or expression, or treatment at port of entry; those visitor-facing questions are not sourced.

Information on the availability of gender-affirming healthcare, including whether access is restricted by law, is not covered by these sources.
